title: Obituary: Gloria Steinem
gist: An obituary of second-wave feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died on 2 September 2026 aged 92, traces her founding of Ms. magazine in 1972 and her decades of activism, while noting the author's own view that Steinem's death comes amid a 'savagery of the current backlash against feminism' epitomised by the overturning of Roe v Wade in 2022 and the fact America still has never elected a female president.

themes.theme: Steinem's career and Ms. magazine as a media/business case study

insights.claim: Gloria Steinem launched Ms. magazine in 1972 as a standalone publication after it first appeared as an insert in New York magazine in 1971; deliberately dated 'spring 1972' so it could stay on newsstands for months, the first issue nonetheless sold out in just eight days.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
insights.so_what: A historical case study in identifying an underserved media market (a magazine 'run by and for women' with no advertising for housewife products) and achieving immediate demand validation -- a durable example of niche-audience media product-market fit.

insights.claim: Steinem edited Ms. magazine for 15 years while simultaneously building a political and activist career, including co-founding the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971 and campaigning for the Equal Rights Amendment (first introduced to Congress in 1923 and still not ratified).
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
insights.so_what: Notes that the ERA, first proposed in 1923, remains unratified over a century later -- illustrating how slow-moving US constitutional/legal change can be even on causes with sustained multi-decade organized advocacy.

insights.claim: The obituary's author explicitly frames Steinem's death as occurring amid 'the savagery of the current backlash against feminism,' citing the 2022 overturning of Roe v Wade and the fact that the US has still never elected a female president as evidence that gains from the second-wave era are being rolled back or remain incomplete.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
insights.so_what: Signals that mainstream commentary is actively framing US reproductive-rights and gender-representation trends as a structural 'backlash' period rather than a temporary setback -- relevant context for assessing durability of reproductive-rights-related state legislation and its economic/social effects (e.g. interstate migration for care access, corporate policy responses).
insights.quote: Despite the savagery of the current backlash against feminism, her joy and optimism are evident from the very first page.

insights.claim: Steinem herself said in an interview shortly before her death: 'I never expected Trump. And that we still haven't had a female president — I would not have expected that,' indicating she viewed both outcomes as having defied the trajectory she expected from the movement's progress.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
insights.so_what: A first-person acknowledgment from a leading feminist figure that the movement's assumed linear-progress trajectory (culminating in a female president) has not materialized, tempering narratives of inevitable social progress on gender representation in US politics.
insights.quote: I never expected Trump. And that we still haven't had a female president — I would not have expected that.
insights.locator: paragraph near the end quoting Steinem on Trump

themes.theme: Critiques of Steinem's brand of feminism

insights.claim: While no one doubted Steinem's commitment to women's rights broadly, critics accused her of overlooking intersecting discriminations, characterizing her as the face of a liberal feminism that privileged white, conventionally attractive women and had significant blind spots.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
insights.so_what: Signals a durable internal fault line within feminist movements (intersectionality vs. a more singular gender-focused liberal feminism) that continues to shape debates over representation and messaging in current advocacy organizations.
insights.quote: For them, she was the face of a brand of liberal feminism that privileged white, good-looking women above all, and which had plenty of blind spots.
